summary: Within a painted circle, a young shepherd in a short belted tunic stands with a sheep across his shoulders while another animal stands at his feet, framed by slender plants. The image, among the oldest in the Crypt of Lucina, expresses in the simplest pastoral language the hope of the Christians buried here: that Christ, the Good Shepherd, would carry them home.
facts: The Crypt of Lucina is one of the earliest nuclei of the Catacomb of Callixtus on the Via Appia; Commons and Wilpert date its paintings to the late 2nd or early 3rd century.
This image is Wilpert's 1903 black-and-white photographic plate (pl. 35); the painting is distinct from the better-known coloured Good Shepherd with a milk pail in the same catacomb.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and in some cases hand-coloured.
notes: The ram-bearer (kriophoros) type was also used in pagan funerary art; in the Christian setting of the Crypt of Lucina it is generally read as Christ the Good Shepherd, though the identification is an interpretation of a symbolic image.

summary: On a damaged, pale wall two faint red-brown figures can be made out: a larger man reaching out to a smaller, naked figure who stands in water. The scene is commonly identified as John the Baptist baptizing Christ, which would make it one of the very earliest surviving images of the Baptism, though the painting is now very faded.
facts: Commons records this painting in the Crypt of Lucina, the oldest part of the Catacomb of Callixtus.
In early Christian art the baptized Christ is usually shown small and naked, standing in the water, with the Baptist larger beside him – the convention visible here.
notes: Whether this baptism shows Christ or represents the sacrament of baptism in general is debated; no dove is clearly visible in the surviving paint.

summary: In a small lunette a pale lamb stands before a row of baskets of bread and touches them with a rod, the gesture with which Christ is shown multiplying the loaves on contemporary sarcophagi. Here Christ appears in the guise of the Lamb of God, performing the miracle of the loaves – a compact image that unites the sacrifice of Christ with the gift of the Eucharistic bread.
facts: Commons gives its size as only 40 × 28 cm and dates it to the mid-4th century.
The rod (virga) touching the baskets is the standard sign of Christ's miracle-working in 4th-century Roman art, transferred here to the Lamb.
notes: The Lamb is a symbolic image of Christ; the identification of the scene with the multiplication of the loaves rests on the iconography.

summary: In a long frieze the Virgin sits enthroned at the centre with the Christ Child on her lap, while Magi in short tunics and Phrygian caps approach from both sides bearing gifts. The symmetrical arrangement – unusual in having four Magi rather than three – shows the painter freely shaping the Gospel scene to suit the space while keeping the Child at its heart.
facts: Matthew does not number the Magi; early catacomb painters show two, three or, as here, four of them, the number of three becoming standard only later.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

summary: Wilpert's photograph shows the damaged vault of a small chamber painted with concentric circles and compartments; in the central field Christ sits as judge, with figures turned towards him in the surrounding fields. The chamber took its name from this vault painting, an early attempt to picture the judgment of the soul by Christ.
facts: Italian Wikipedia calls the main monument of this small rural catacomb the 'cubiculum of the Judgment', fully painted and dating to the second half of the 3rd century.
The catacomb was discovered by Giovanni Battista de Rossi in 1877; it contains no martyrs' tombs and served a small rural community.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903) (plate 75).
notes: Much of the vault is lost; the identification of the central figure as Christ the Judge follows Wilpert and later scholarship.

summary: A detached, badly damaged fresco shows a row of five nimbed figures standing frontally against a light ground; the figure at the centre is Christ, flanked by four nimbed saints, probably the local martyrs. The painting – known as the 'crowning of the martyrs' – shows Christ welcoming and rewarding the saints whose tomb drew pilgrims to this small catacomb.
facts: The fresco is displayed as a detached panel, mounted in a frame, as the photograph shows.
notes: Commons supplies no description beyond the title 'coronatio martyrum'; the date and the names of the flanking saints are given here only in general terms. The image is small (460 px).

summary: A ceiling decorated with red lines, garlands and small birds centres on a medallion in which the Good Shepherd stands among his sheep, a lamb across his shoulders. A crack runs across the vault, but the gentle, airy decoration still conveys the peace and paradise-garden imagery with which Roman Christians surrounded their dead.
facts: Commons and Wilpert date the painting to the second half of the 3rd century.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.
notes: The Good Shepherd in funerary art is a symbolic image whose identification with Christ is an interpretation; in this Christian catacomb it is generally accepted.

summary: A cross-vault is divided into painted fields: at the centre the Good Shepherd carries a sheep, surrounded by Jonah resting under his vine, Adam and Eve, a praying orans and decorative motifs. The programme gathers images of salvation around Christ the Shepherd, who stands in the very centre of the ceiling above the dead.
facts: According to the Commons description of Wilpert's plate 171, the centre shows the Good Shepherd, the right Jonah in repose, the left Adam and Eve, and the bottom an orans.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.
notes: As elsewhere, the Good Shepherd is read as a symbol of Christ in this Christian context.

summary: In an arcosolium lunette a veiled woman with large eyes raises her hands in prayer, a child placed before her breast, between two chi-rho monograms. The painting has long been celebrated as one of the earliest images of the Virgin Mary with the Christ Child in prayer, a forerunner of the later 'Virgin of the Sign'.
facts: The chi-rho monograms – the first letters of Christ's name in Greek – flank the figure on both sides.
Commons classifies the image among 4th-century paintings of the Madonna and Child and among images of the 'Theotokos of the Sign' type.
notes: Many scholars think the woman may be the deceased with her child rather than the Virgin and Christ; the identification remains uncertain.

summary: A naked young figure stands frontally in the water while, above him, the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from the top left. The scene is the Baptism of Christ, painted in the shorthand of the catacombs: the Baptist is reduced to a hand and part of a figure at the upper edge, and everything centres on the Son on whom the Spirit rests.
facts: The descending dove distinguishes the Baptism of Christ from ordinary baptism scenes in catacomb painting.
The Catacomb of Marcellinus and Peter on the Via Labicana covers about three hectares with 4.5 km of galleries on three levels.
notes: Commons gives no date or provenance details for this file; the date given here is approximate.

summary: Within concentric painted octagons on a ceiling, the Good Shepherd stands between two trees, a sheep on his shoulders and a vessel in his hand, with sheep at his feet. The geometric frame turns the ceiling into a window onto the green pastures promised to the faithful.
facts: Commons places this painting in the Catacomb of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; an early photograph of the same ceiling appears in 'Monuments of the Early Church' (1901).
The Catacomb of Marcellinus and Peter preserves an unusually rich cycle of 3rd–4th-century paintings.
notes: The Good Shepherd is read as Christ in this Christian context; the date is approximate.

summary: Wilpert's plate shows a whole painted chamber: in the arcosolium at the back the Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin and Child, while the surrounding walls and ceiling carry orantes, Jonah, Moses striking the rock and Noah in the ark. The Epiphany is set among Old Testament images of deliverance, as the first revelation of Christ to the nations.
facts: According to the Commons description, the scenes from top are orants, Jonah and the whale, Moses striking the rock, Noah praying in the ark and the Adoration of the Magi.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

summary: A bearded Christ with long dark hair and a large nimbus looks out frontally, his right hand raised, the letters Alpha and Omega painted at either side. Unlike the youthful shepherd of earlier catacomb art, this is the majestic, bearded Christ of the late 4th century, proclaimed as the beginning and the end.
facts: Commons dates the painting to the late 4th or early 5th century.
The Alpha and Omega, from Revelation, became a common attribute of Christ in late 4th-century Roman art.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

summary: Christ appears as a frontal bust with a cross-nimbus, large eyes, short beard and long hair, set within an arched frame above a painted inscription. The austere, hieratic face belongs to the age of icons and shows how the catacombs continued to be decorated for pilgrims long after burials there had ceased.
facts: Commons dates the painting to about the 6th–7th century, from Wilpert's 1903 plate.
The Catacomb of Pontian, on the Via Portuense, is also known for a painted baptistery and frescoes of the martyrs Abdon and Sennen.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

summary: A seated woman holds a child at her breast, while a man beside her raises his hand and points upward, towards a star painted above (outside this crop). The image is usually read as the Virgin nursing the Christ Child with a prophet – Balaam or Isaiah – foretelling his birth, and it is counted among the oldest surviving images of Mary and Jesus.
facts: English Wikipedia notes that the Priscilla catacomb 'may contain the oldest known Marian paintings, from the early third century'.
Commons identifies the pointing man as either Balaam, whose prophecy speaks of a star, or Isaiah, who foretold the birth from a virgin.

summary: Against a light ground a young, beardless Christ in a long tunic and pallium bends forward and touches with a rod a row of seven baskets of bread at his feet. With a single figure and a row of baskets the painter evokes the feeding of the multitude, a sign of the Eucharist and of the heavenly banquet.
facts: The rod with which Christ touches the baskets is the usual sign of miraculous power in 4th-century Roman art.
The catacomb on the Via Anapo is anonymous: its ancient name is not known.

summary: Wilpert's plate shows a painted arcosolium: in the lunette Christ sits among saints, while scenes of Moses and Jonah appear on the surrounding wall and arch. The tomb places its occupant under the protection of Christ enthroned in the company of the saints.
facts: Wilpert's caption reads 'Moses, Jonah, Christ with saints'.
The catacomb of Cyriaca lies beneath San Lorenzo fuori le mura; Italian Wikipedia notes that wartime bombing and the Verano cemetery have left it in poor condition.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.
notes: The plate is small and the central figures are hard to read; date approximate.

summary: Two crowded registers flank a shell medallion with the portraits of a married couple. Above, the creation of Eve and Christ with Adam and Eve are followed by Christ's miracles at Cana, of the loaves and of Lazarus; below, the Magi adore the Child on Mary's lap, Christ heals the blind man and foretells Peter's denial. The sarcophagus sets the whole story of salvation, from creation to resurrection, around the hope of the dead couple.
facts: It was found in the 19th century during rebuilding at San Paolo fuori le Mura and is catalogued as Vatican 104.
Its name comes from the scene of three similar figures creating Eve, read as an allusion to the Trinity and the doctrine of the Council of Nicaea (325).
Wikipedia notes stylistic links with the reliefs added to the Arch of Constantine (315), suggesting a related workshop.

summary: A shell medallion with two male portraits divides two dense registers of biblical scenes: Christ raising Lazarus, multiplying the loaves and healing the blind, Peter's denial and arrest, Daniel among the lions and Abraham's sacrifice. Its deep carving and crowded, lively figures make it one of the finest double-register sarcophagi of Constantinian Rome.
facts: The name comes from the two male busts in the central shell, generally taken as brothers buried together.
Commons records its provenance as the 'cimitero di Lucina' and dates it about 325–350.

summary: Under a lid inscribed for the married couple Agape and Crescentianus, the chest is divided by twisted columns and gables into seven niches, each holding a biblical scene with Christ, the apostles or Old Testament figures. The architectural frame lends each episode the dignity of a small shrine.
facts: The lid inscription begins 'CONIVGI CARISSIMAE AGAPENI', naming Agape, who was buried by her husband Crescentianus.
Commons records the sarcophagus as coming from the Vatican necropolis.
notes: The individual scenes in each niche have not been verified one by one here.

summary: The front is dominated by a lively seascape telling the story of Jonah – thrown overboard, swallowed and cast up by the sea-monster, and resting under his vine. Around it are smaller scenes including Christ raising Lazarus from his tomb and Moses striking the rock. Jonah's three days in the monster were read by Christ himself as a sign of his resurrection, here paired with the raising of Lazarus.
facts: Commons dates the front to about 280–300 and records its provenance as the Vatican necropolis.
Its date makes it one of the earliest sarcophagi with explicit Christian narrative, made before the Peace of the Church (313).
notes: Christ appears in the small raising of Lazarus at the upper left; the Jonah cycle forms most of the relief.

summary: Three shepherds carrying sheep stand on pedestals at the ends and centre, while the whole surface between them is filled with vines in which winged putti harvest and tread the grapes. The vintage, a symbol of the Eucharist and of paradise, surrounds the Good Shepherd, the image of Christ caring for the souls of the dead.
facts: The sarcophagus is displayed in the Museo Pio Cristiano and dated by Commons to the second half of the 4th century.
The motif of the grape harvest by putti was shared with pagan Dionysiac art and given new meaning in Christian use.
notes: The Good Shepherd figures are symbolic; their identification with Christ is an interpretation, well established in this Christian context.

summary: Between ram-headed ends, a seated philosopher reading and a praying woman flank a central shepherd carrying a sheep, with other figures in a tranquil landscape. The sarcophagus speaks Christian hope in a language its pagan neighbours would have recognised: the Good Shepherd stands at the centre between learning and prayer.
facts: It is dated by the Museo Pio Cristiano to about 250–275 (inv. 31540), before the Peace of the Church.
Commons describes it as 'crypto-Christian': its imagery could be read by pagans as philosophical and bucolic and by Christians as Christ the Good Shepherd.
notes: Whether the patrons were Christian is debated; the central shepherd is included here as a probable image of Christ the Good Shepherd.

summary: The Virgin, veiled and seated, holds up the Child, who stretches out his hands to receive the gifts of three Magi in short tunics and Phrygian caps; a star shines above, and the heads of their camels appear behind them. The Child's eager gesture makes this one of the most tender versions of the scene in early Christian sculpture.
facts: Commons states that the panel comes from a Roman sarcophagus found in the cemetery of Sant'Agnese in Rome.
The camels' heads in the background are a characteristic detail of Roman Epiphany scenes.

summary: A continuous frieze of tightly packed figures runs across the front: Christ performs miracles among the apostles, and at the right end he rides on a donkey into Jerusalem while a man spreads his garment before him. The relief reads like a pageant of Christ's saving works culminating in his royal entry.
facts: Commons records that the sarcophagus comes from the Coemeterium Maius on the Via Nomentana.
Continuous frieze sarcophagi of this kind were the commonest type of Christian sarcophagus in Constantinian Rome.

summary: Short, curly-haired figures crowd the front in a single frieze. According to the museum label recorded on Commons, it shows the sacrifice of Isaac, the healing of the blind man, the healing of the paralytic, the multiplication of the loaves and fishes and further healings. The repeated image of the young Christ touching and restoring the sick gave the bereaved a vivid hope of resurrection.
facts: Commons dates it to about 300–330, the very beginning of the Constantinian period.
The naked figures at the right belong to the Adam and Eve scene, a frequent companion of the miracles on these sarcophagi.

summary: In one arched niche of a columnar sarcophagus, the young Christ, his hair falling to his shoulders, stands between two bearded apostles who hold out loaves and fish; baskets of bread stand at their feet. The calm, classical carving of the later 4th century gives the miracle the solemnity of a liturgical offering.
facts: Commons dates the sarcophagus to about 350–375; this image shows a detail of its front.
The beardless, long-haired Christ is typical of Theodosian-era sculpture.

summary: Two registers of biblical scenes surround a shell medallion holding the portraits of a couple. Christ appears repeatedly as miracle-worker among the apostles, alongside Old Testament scenes and episodes from the life of Peter.
facts: Commons notes restorations by the 18th-century sculptor-restorer Bartolomeo Cavaceppi.
It belongs to the double-register type with a central clipeus, like the Dogmatic Sarcophagus in the same museum.
notes: Individual scenes have not been verified one by one; parts are 18th-century restoration.

summary: A married couple is portrayed in the central shell; around them, on two levels, crowds of small figures enact biblical scenes, including Christ raising Lazarus from an aedicula-tomb. The sarcophagus shows how Roman workshops multiplied the same repertoire of saving miracles for Christian families of the 4th century.
facts: Commons records its provenance as the cemetery of San Callisto on the Via Appia.
A separate Commons photograph details its raising of Lazarus.

summary: A circular medallion with the busts of a couple – their faces left unfinished – divides two registers of biblical scenes in which Christ heals, multiplies the loaves and raises the dead. The blank faces show that such sarcophagi were carved in advance and personalised (or not) when bought.
facts: The Commons description notes the 'clipeo (busti non finiti)', the unfinished portrait busts.
Commons dates it to about 300–330.

summary: Around a shell with the portraits of a couple, two registers present miracles of Christ, scenes of Peter and Old Testament types of salvation in tight succession. Parts of the relief are restorations, but the composition preserves the full Constantinian programme of Christian hope.
facts: According to Commons, it was found in 1592 in the Vigna Guidaschi near San Sebastiano on the Via Appia.
Commons notes that the front is partly restored.
notes: Commons gives the date variously as '330–25' (file name) and 300–330 (description).

summary: At the left of this fragment, the young Christ, holding a scroll, reaches towards the swaddled Lazarus standing in his temple-like tomb, while Martha kneels at his feet; to the right, soldiers lead Peter away under arrest and a cock recalls his denial. The carving is crisp and expressive, the faces individualised.
facts: The museum describes the scenes as the raising of Lazarus, the arrest of Peter, and an orans reworked as the denial of Peter.
The small cockerel at the lower right alludes to Christ's prophecy of Peter's denial.

summary: A shepherd in a short tunic and leggings carries a large ram across his shoulders and leans on a knotted staff. The statue served as the support of a marble table, and its sturdy, frontal figure shows the Good Shepherd entering the repertoire of Christian sculpture in the round.
facts: The museum label describes it as the base of a lost marble altar or table, with the legs and the lamb's muzzle remodelled; its provenance is unknown.
It is displayed near the celebrated Good Shepherd statue in the same museum.
notes: The ram-bearer was a familiar pagan figure; its Christian meaning here is inferred from its context in the Christian collections and is not certain.

summary: Daniel stands naked between two lions, his arms raised in prayer, while at the right Christ, holding a long rod, touches the mummy-like Lazarus standing in a columned tomb on a brick podium. The two deliverances – from the lions and from death – are set side by side as promises of salvation.
facts: Commons places this relief among the Roman sarcophagi of the Museo Pio Cristiano.
The temple-front tomb raised on steps is the standard way of showing Lazarus's grave in Roman art.
notes: Inventory number not confirmed; date approximate.

summary: A long frieze shows the youthful Christ performing miracles – at Cana, of the loaves, healing the blind, raising Lazarus – and foretelling Peter's denial, while the lid holds one of the earliest Nativity scenes, with the Child watched by the ox, the ass and a shepherd. Old and New Testament scenes are interwoven, presenting Christ as a teacher-philosopher with wonder-working power.
facts: It was found in 1884 in Via della Lungara, near San Giacomo in Settimiana; the lid inscription names Lucius Valerius Claudius Maximus Claudianus, who died aged about 43.
Italian Wikipedia notes that it, with the Stilicho sarcophagus in Milan, preserves two of the earliest Nativity scenes, in which the Child appears without Mary and Joseph.

summary: This tub-shaped sarcophagus unfolds from left to right: a ship and Jonah cast up by the sea-monster, Jonah resting, a praying woman, a seated philosopher reading, the Good Shepherd, and the Baptism of a small naked Christ, closing with fishermen casting a net. It is one of the earliest sarcophagi to tell the Christian story, combining the old pastoral images with a Gospel scene.
facts: The Commons description lists the scenes as ship, Jonah, sheep, orans, seated man with a scroll, Christ the Good Shepherd, the Baptism of Christ and two fishermen (perhaps Peter and Andrew).
Commons dates it to about 275, which would make it earlier than the Peace of the Church.
notes: The identification of the baptism as Christ's own is generally accepted but not certain.

summary: Against a backdrop of city walls and gates, Christ stands at the centre on the hill of paradise, handing the scroll of the Law to Peter, while the other apostles approach from both sides in a stately procession. The 'city-gate' background evokes the heavenly Jerusalem into which the apostles – and the deceased – are received.
facts: Commons records that it came from the mausoleum of the Anicii beneath St Peter's in the Vatican.
The Traditio Legis, Christ giving the law to Peter, was a favourite theme of late-4th-century Roman art.

summary: Christ sits enthroned at the centre, raising his hand as he teaches, while the apostles sit on either side in two animated rows, scrolls in hand, turning towards him. The composition, taken from images of philosophers and their pupils, proclaims Christ as the one true Teacher.
facts: Commons records that it was found at Rignieux-le-Franc (Ain), in eastern France.
The Louvre's photographer describes the main face as 'Christ enthroned at the centre teaching the apostles'.

summary: Olive trees with interlacing branches divide the front into five scenes from the Old and New Testaments, among which Christ appears as miracle-worker. The trees turn the series of episodes into a walk through the garden of paradise.
facts: The Louvre catalogues it as a 'sarcophage à arbres', a type in which trees replace columns as dividers.
Commons dates it to the first half of the 4th century.
notes: The individual scenes were not verified one by one.

summary: Panels of vine scrolls, flowers and fruit alternate with three framed figures: at the centre Christ, flanked by two apostles. The flat, ornamental carving shows how the Christian sarcophagus survived into the 6th century in Gaul, with Christ still at the centre of the tomb.
facts: The Louvre catalogue entry recorded on Commons gives its size as 49 × 201 × 70 cm and its provenance as Castelnau-de-Guers (Hérault).
It has been exhibited at the Louvre-Lens in the 'Galerie du Temps'.

summary: Between bands of strigils, a simple incised panel names Livia Primitiva, who died aged 24 years and 9 months, and below it shows the Good Shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders between two others, accompanied by a fish and an anchor. Modest as it is, it is one of the earliest objects to declare its owner's Christian faith openly.
facts: Its inscription records that Livia Nicarus made it for her sister Livia Primitiva.
Commons notes that the Good Shepherd, the fish and the anchor together show that the deceased belonged to the Christian community.
notes: The Good Shepherd is a symbolic image of Christ; here the fish and anchor make the Christian reading clear.

summary: Under a lid carved with small scenes and an inscription, Christ sits enthroned at the centre of an arcaded colonnade, surrounded by the apostles seated in pairs on either side. The ordered, symmetrical composition presents Christ as the heavenly ruler and teacher of the apostolic college.
facts: The museum dates it to 380/390; it is carved from Carrara marble.
Commons has a separate photograph of the inscription on its lid, from which the sarcophagus takes the name of Concordius.
notes: The apostles are not individually identifiable in the photograph.

summary: Trees divide the front into niches where Christ, the apostles and the recipients of his miracles appear; among the scenes is the Wedding at Cana, where Christ touches the water jars with his rod. The leafy canopy evokes paradise as the setting of Christ's saving deeds.
facts: Commons notes that in the 18th century the sarcophagus was displayed in the archbishop's palace in Arles (FAN.92.00.2488).
It is carved from Proconnesian marble from the Sea of Marmara.

summary: A praying woman with raised arms stands at the centre of a crowded frieze in which Christ performs miracles among the apostles. The orans – the image of the soul in prayer – is placed literally in the midst of Christ's saving acts.
facts: The museum calls it the 'Sarcophage de l'Orante'.
Arles possesses the largest collection of early Christian sarcophagi outside Rome.
notes: Date approximate; individual scenes not verified.

summary: Two registers of figures surround a shell with the portraits of a couple; the lower register is filled by the sea and the story of Jonah, while elsewhere Christ appears among the apostles performing miracles. Jonah's deliverance, a sign of the resurrection, is joined to the miracles of Christ.
facts: The museum names it after the story of Jonah, which occupies much of the lower register.
Its two-register layout with a central shell is the Roman type also seen on the Dogmatic Sarcophagus.
notes: Date approximate; the Christ scenes were not individually verified.

summary: Two fields of wavy strigils frame a central panel in two tiers showing the Nativity, with further figures at the corners. The rippling strigils, a decoration inherited from pagan sarcophagi, give way at the centre to the birth of Christ.
facts: The museum states that it is carved from marble of Saint-Béat in the Pyrenees and dates from the end of the 4th century.
Its use of Pyrenean marble points to a regional workshop rather than an import from Rome.

summary: In the left panel of this strigilated front, Christ speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well, whose wheel and rope are carved beside her; below is a further scene with Christ. The quiet conversation at the well recalls the promise of the 'living water' of eternal life.
facts: The museum calls it 'part of a strigilated sarcophagus called the Samaritan Woman'.
Scenes were often placed only in the end panels of strigilated sarcophagi, leaving the centre to the wavy strigils.
notes: Date approximate.

summary: A continuous frieze of figures shows Christ working miracles among the apostles together with scenes of Peter, from whom the sarcophagus takes its name. Dense and animated, it reflects the Roman Constantinian style that spread to Arles.
facts: The museum dates it to the 330s.
Its traditional name refers to a scene of Peter, the founder of the Roman see.
notes: Scenes not verified one by one.

summary: A crowded relief shows Christ at the centre among the apostles who press around him, with smaller figures kneeling below. The museum identifies the subject as Christ's farewell to his apostles.
facts: The museum describes the piece as an 'element of a sarcophagus representing Christ's farewell to his apostles'.
A separate small fragment is mounted at its upper left.
notes: The identification of the subject follows the museum's title.

summary: Two fields of strigils separate three standing figures: Christ in the centre and, at the ends, Saints Peter and Paul. The austere design focuses attention on Christ and the two princes of the apostles who founded the Roman Church.
facts: The museum states that it represents Christ at the centre with Saints Peter and Paul at the ends, and dates it to the end of the 4th century.

summary: Between two fields of strigils, the central niche holds Christ with a nimbus, standing and holding an open book; apostles stand in the end panels. The halo – still a novelty in Christian art of the late 4th century – marks Christ out as divine.
facts: The museum names it 'Sarcophagus of the nimbed Christ' and dates it to the end of the 4th century.
The nimbus came into use for Christ in the course of the 4th century.

summary: In this fragment the Good Shepherd stands among bearded apostles, a sheep across his shoulders, between trees with spreading branches. Here the shepherd figure has been absorbed into a Gospel scene with the apostles, making its reference to Christ explicit.
facts: The museum describes it as a fragment of a sarcophagus showing the Good Shepherd with the sheep on his shoulders.
notes: Date approximate.

summary: Seven arched niches separated by columns each hold a standing, bearded figure; Christ stands at the centre among the apostles, several of whom carry offerings. The museum's name, 'the Eucharist', reflects the offering of gifts that runs through the procession.
facts: The museum calls it the 'Eucharistic sarcophagus' and dates it to the end of the 4th century.
notes: The identification of the central figure as Christ and of the Eucharistic theme follows the museum's naming; the figures are worn.

summary: A central medallion with a couple's portraits divides two registers of crowded scenes, among them the story of Susanna, from which the sarcophagus is named, and miracles of Christ. Susanna, saved from false accusation, and the healed and raised of the Gospels speak together of God's deliverance.
facts: The museum states that it is carved from Carrara marble and represents the story of chaste Susanna.
notes: Christ scenes not individually verified.

summary: Three tiers of richly carved figures – lid and two registers of the chest – surround a shell with the portraits of a married couple. The scenes include the creation of Adam and Eve by three figures (whence the name 'of the Trinity'), Christ's miracles and episodes of Peter. It is among the finest Roman imports at Arles.
facts: It was discovered in 1974 and measures 103 × 205 × 111 cm, according to the museum.
Like the Dogmatic Sarcophagus in the Vatican, it shows the creation scene with three similar figures, often read as the Trinity.

summary: Under a lid with a central inscription and scenes of the Nativity and the Magi, the front unrolls a long frieze of miracles, with Christ repeatedly touching and healing among the crowd. It was made for a woman named Marcia Romania Celsa.
facts: The museum states that it was discovered in 1974, like the 'Trinity' sarcophagus.
Its lid combines an inscription panel with small figured scenes, a common arrangement on Roman frieze sarcophagi.
notes: Christ scenes not individually verified.

summary: Five arched niches frame the scenes; at the centre Christ stands on the hill of paradise with its four rivers and hands the unrolled scroll of the Law to Peter, while Paul acclaims him. Other niches show further biblical scenes with the apostles. The Traditio Legis presents Christ as the lawgiver of the new covenant.
facts: Commons records that it comes from the Alyscamps cemetery of Arles and is carved from Carrara marble (FAN.92.00.2487).
A second Commons photograph of the same sarcophagus (Arles sarcophagus with christ.jpg) shows it from a different angle.

summary: Three arches on columns frame the scene: at the centre Christ, bearded and nimbed with a cross above, stands with arms outstretched, while two apostles approach from either side, one carrying a cross. Reused as an altar front, the sarcophagus still sets Christ in glory above the altar.
facts: It was made for Paulus Geminus, administrator of the treasury of the Five Provinces of Gaul, according to the Commons description.
It now supports the altar of the Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre in the former cathedral of Saint-Trophime.
notes: The central figure's identification as Christ is clear from the cross; the side figures are probably Peter and Paul.

summary: Twisted columns and alternating gables and arches form a row of niches, each holding a bearded apostle, with Christ at the centre. Although damaged at the ends, the front preserves the solemn rhythm of a Theodosian columnar sarcophagus.
facts: Commons records that the front came from Genzano near Rome and is in the Musée des Beaux-Arts of Lyon (1937-52).
notes: Date approximate.

summary: Trees separate the scenes of this fragment: at the left Christ heals the blind Bartimaeus, at the centre he stands between Saints Peter and Paul, and at the right appears the tree with the serpent. It was found reused in the walls of a house in Narbonne.
facts: Commons states that it was reused within the walls of the Viguier de l'Estagnol house (rue Viollet-le-Duc) in Narbonne.
It is now displayed in the Narbo Via museum.

summary: On the far left Christ raises the son of a widow; beside him stands a figure between two saints, perhaps the deceased; then Christ multiplies the loaves, followed by Moses at the altar and Moses receiving the tablets of the Law. Old and New Testament are again set side by side.
facts: The fragment was found at Bédoin (Vaucluse) and belongs to the British Museum (1993,0406.1).
It was photographed while on loan to the 'Eye to Eye with the Romans' exhibition at the Gallo-Roman Museum, Tongeren, in 2021.

summary: Beneath the Romanesque pulpit of Sant'Ambrogio, the sarcophagus shows Christ seated among his apostles before a city gate, with twelve sheep below, while other faces show Christ giving the law to Peter and the sacrifice of Isaac; the lid includes the Magi and an early Nativity. It is among the most refined sarcophagi of the Theodosian age.
facts: Wikipedia dates it to about 387–390, two decades before the general Stilicho's death, so it is unlikely to have been his.
It has served as the base of the pulpit of Sant'Ambrogio since before the 10th century.
Its carving has been estimated to have cost 50,000–100,000 Diocletianic denarii.

summary: A shell with the portraits of Adelphia and her husband divides two registers crowded with scenes: Christ heals the woman with the issue of blood and the blind man, multiplies the loaves, raises the widow's son, changes water into wine at Cana and enters Jerusalem, while the Magi adore the Child. It is the masterpiece of Christian sculpture in Sicily.
facts: It was found in 1872 in the Rotunda of Adelphia in the Catacombs of San Giovanni, Syracuse.
The lid inscription reads 'Here lies Adelfia, clarissima femina, wife of Count Valerius'.

summary: In a calm, spacious composition Christ, nimbed and standing on a mound, hands the Law to an apostle, between palms and further figures; the ends of the chest show Daniel among the lions and the raising of Lazarus. The broad, airy design is typical of the sculpture of Ravenna in its imperial age.
facts: The museum label recorded on Commons gives its provenance as the church of San Giovanni Battista, Ravenna, and dates it to the early 5th century.
Commons has separate photographs of its Daniel and Lazarus scenes.

summary: Between two palm trees, Christ sits enthroned at the centre while two apostles approach from either side; the curved lid bears a later inscription naming the Pignatta family who reused the tomb. Set in the open air near Dante's tomb, it is one of the Ravennate sarcophagi in which Christ reigns between palms of paradise.
facts: Commons records the front as showing 'the enthroned Christ' (Die Frontseite ... den thronenden Christus darstellend).
The lid inscription records its reuse by the Pignatta family.
notes: Date approximate.

summary: On the front, three Magi in fluttering cloaks hurry with their gifts towards the Virgin, who holds the Christ Child on her lap at the left. The sarcophagus, carved in the 5th century, was reused in the 7th for the Armenian exarch Isaac, and its lively relief contrasts with the sober barrel-vaulted lid.
facts: Isaac the Armenian was exarch of Ravenna (c. 625–643); his tomb is in San Vitale.
Wikipedia notes that the sarcophagus also shows Daniel and Lazarus.
notes: The 5th-century date of the carving is the usual view; the reuse dates to Isaac's death.

summary: Between palm trees, Christ is seated at the centre holding a book, while Peter and Paul bow towards him from either side, offering wreaths. The scaly, rounded lid is typical of Ravenna. Carved in the 5th century, the sarcophagus was later reused for the 14th-century archbishop Rinaldo da Concorreggio.
facts: Commons dates the sarcophagus to the 5th century; Rinaldo da Concorreggio was archbishop of Ravenna (died 1321).
It stands in the Chapel of the Madonna del Sudore in the cathedral.
notes: The apostles' identification as Peter and Paul is the usual reading.

summary: A continuous frieze of short, sturdy figures shows biblical scenes, with Christ healing and working miracles among the apostles and other figures. Imported from Rome, it shows how early Christian sarcophagi reached the far northwest of the Iberian Peninsula.
facts: The museum dates it to about 310 and states that it comes from Astorga cathedral; Commons associates it with San Justo de la Vega (León).
It is catalogued in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional as inv. 50310.
notes: Individual scenes not verified.

summary: Columns divide the front into niches with Old and New Testament scenes – among them the Fall of Adam and Eve and Moses striking the rock – and the deceased, alongside scenes of Christ. Found in Córdoba itself, it is one of the finest early Christian sarcophagi in Spain.
facts: The museum dates it to the first third of the 4th century and records that it was found in the city of Córdoba.
Commons has detailed photographs of its Original Sin and Moses scenes.
notes: The Christ scenes were not individually verified.

summary: Set into the cathedral façade, the front shows five scenes from left to right: the healing of the blind, the healing of the woman with the issue of blood, the healing of the paralytic at the pool of Bethesda – shown in two tiers – the encounter with Zacchaeus and Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
facts: The healing at the pool of Bethesda is carved in two tiers at the centre, giving the front its name.
This example is built into the façade of Tarragona cathedral above the right side door.

summary: Under an ornate architrave on twisted columns, a youthful Christ stands frontally between two apostles, his right hand raised. The relief was carved in Constantinople by reworking an older pagan columnar sarcophagus from Dokimeion in Asia Minor, a striking example of the Christian transformation of classical monuments.
facts: The museum states that it was acquired in Istanbul in 1899 (inv. 2430).
The original 3rd-century sarcophagus came from the marble workshops of Dokimeion in Phrygia.

summary: At the left a praying woman appears in a round medallion; beside it Christ, among bearded apostles holding loaves, multiplies the bread, with baskets at the base. The deeply undercut heads and drapery give the relief a vivid immediacy.
facts: The museum dates it to about 330 (inv. 1501).

summary: Columns and a central gabled aedicula articulate the front: in the middle the Good Shepherd stands with a sheep on his shoulders, flanked by the deceased couple in the side niches and by crowds of small figures. The tomb comes from Salona, the great early Christian centre of Dalmatia.
facts: It comes from Salona and is dated by Commons to about 300–330.
Salona, near Split, was the capital of Roman Dalmatia and the seat of an important early Christian community.
notes: The Good Shepherd is a symbolic image of Christ; here the Christian context of the Salona cemeteries supports the identification.

summary: Five arched niches on twisted columns each frame a New Testament scene with Christ – among them his miracles of healing and his encounters with his disciples. The calm, classical figures are typical of late-4th-century Rome.
facts: Commons records that this sarcophagus once belonged to the painter Peter Paul Rubens.
It is now in the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden (National Museum of Antiquities) in Leiden.
notes: The five scenes were not identified individually here.

summary: In the central medallion a husband and wife are crowned by a small figure of Christ above them; around them radiate panels with standing saints and their names, like the spokes of a wheel. Cut from the base of a bowl, such glasses were pressed into the mortar of catacomb tombs as markers and keepsakes.
facts: It was shown at the exhibition 'Pretiosa vitrea' in Florence in 2017–2018.
Gold glass was made by sandwiching cut gold leaf between two layers of fused glass.

summary: Within a ring of gold triangles, Christ raises Lazarus beside a tree; the gold figures are partly obscured by corrosion. The scene of Lazarus, the most frequent Gospel miracle in catacomb art, made this an apt object to set beside a Christian grave.
facts: The Bargello catalogues it as Roman, about 350–400, showing the raising of Lazarus.
Such gold-glass medallions survive mostly because they were embedded in the plaster sealing catacomb tombs.
notes: Surface damage makes the details hard to read; the identification follows the museum.

summary: The bearded busts of Peter and Paul, named in gold letters, face each other while a small standing Christ between them holds wreaths over their heads. A Latin toast runs around the rim, recalling that these were once the bottoms of drinking bowls.
facts: The image of Christ crowning Peter and Paul is common on Roman gold glass, reflecting the cult of the two apostles in Rome.
It was exhibited at 'Pretiosa vitrea', Florence, 2017–2018.

summary: In the central roundel is a bust of Christ, and around it, like rays, stand the twelve apostles, some named in gold letters such as PETRUS. The radiating composition places Christ at the centre of the apostolic college, as the sun among its rays.
facts: Commons places it in the collections of the National Archaeological Museum of Parma and dates it to the 4th–5th century.
notes: The identification of the central bust as Christ follows the museum's title; the glass is cracked.

summary: On a deep blue ground, a tall Christ in tunic and pallium, his name partly legible in the inscription above, stretches out his rod towards the small swaddled figure of Lazarus in a temple-tomb approached by steps. It is one of the finest gold-glass images of the miracle.
facts: The inscription along the upper edge includes the name of Christ (…CRISTVS…).
Commons states that it is in the Vatican's Christian collections.

summary: A central figure is surrounded by a ring of small gold scenes of miracles, arranged around the circular base of a vessel. Such gold-glass bases, decorated with biblical scenes, were treasured in life and set at graves in death.
facts: The Metropolitan Museum titles it 'Bowl Base with Miracle Scenes' and releases its image under CC0.
notes: The individual miracle scenes and the central figure could not be identified from the available photograph; date approximate.
